title: How to Teach Programming in the AI Era? Using LLMs as a Teachable Agent for Debugging
extended_summary:
This paper examines how programming education should adapt in the era of large language models (LLMs), focusing specifically on whether students can be taught to better evaluate and debug AI-generated code. The authors argue that, as LLMs become common "AI pair programmers," students need explicit training in debugging and hypothesis construction rather than only relying on writing code themselves. The central research question is whether students’ debugging skills can be improved through explicit, scaffolded practice with low instructor preparation cost.

To address this, the paper introduces HypoCompass, an LLM-augmented intelligent tutoring system for debugging. In HypoCompass, novice learners role-play as teaching assistants who help LLM-simulated student agents debug buggy code. The system is designed to train two targeted skills: constructing comprehensive hypotheses about possible bugs through test-suite creation, and constructing accurate hypotheses about the cause of observed failures by selecting explanations for bugs. LLMs generate practice materials such as buggy programs, bug explanations, fixes, hints, and immediate feedback, while students focus on the core reasoning tasks rather than code completion. The paper also evaluates the LLM material-generation pipeline itself, showing that it can produce usable instructional materials more efficiently than human teaching assistants.

The learning study involved 19 novice programming learners recruited from four US public and private institutions, including undergraduate and graduate students. Participants completed a pre-survey, pre-test, interaction with HypoCompass, post-test, and post-survey in an approximately one-hour lab-style user study. Quantitatively, students improved their pre- to post-test debugging performance by 11.7% and reduced completion time by 13.6%, with especially strong gains in accurate hypothesis construction. Qualitatively, students reported that the system was engaging, enjoyable, less frustrating than conventional debugging practice, and confidence-building. The paper also includes an LLM evaluation study showing that HypoCompass could generate complete practice sets with high success rates and substantially less time than human material creation.

The main conclusion is that HypoCompass is a promising approach for teaching debugging in the AI era by using LLMs not simply to provide answers, but as imperfect teachable agents that students learn to evaluate. The authors conclude that the system can both reduce instructor workload in generating debugging materials and improve novice learners’ debugging skills, confidence, and engagement. They note, however, that the evidence is based on small, short-term, in-lab studies and that future classroom deployments with controlled comparisons are needed.

identified_tools.name: HypoCompass
identified_tools.description: An LLM-augmented teachable-agent debugging tutor for introductory programming that simulates novice students with buggy code and supports learners in hypothesis construction through test design, bug explanation selection, hints, and immediate feedback.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied as an interactive system for training CS1 novices on debugging, especially comprehensive and accurate hypothesis construction, while using LLMs to generate buggy programs, explanations, fixes, and hints.

findings.finding_summary: In a learning evaluation with 19 novices, students' pre-test to post-test scores significantly improved by 11.7% after using HypoCompass (p = 0.033 < 0.05). The paper reports this as evidence that the system improved transferable debugging skills, using human-generated bugs in the tests rather than the same bugs seen in practice.
findings.measure: Pre-test to post-test debugging assessment score

findings.finding_summary: Students' pre-test to post-test completion time significantly decreased by 13.6% after interacting with HypoCompass (p = 0.003). The authors interpret this as improved debugging proficiency and efficiency on the aligned assessment.
findings.measure: Pre-test to post-test test completion time

findings.finding_summary: For comprehensive hypothesis construction (LO1), the paper reports a 6.1% score improvement and a 23.6% reduction in completion time from pre- to post-test. These analyses are descriptive breakdowns by learning objective; no separate significance test is reported for LO1.
findings.measure: LO1 score and time on comprehensive hypothesis construction items

findings.finding_summary: For accurate hypothesis construction (LO2), the paper reports a 15.8% score improvement and a 9.0% reduction in completion time from pre- to post-test. These breakdowns suggest larger learning gains on LO2 than LO1, though the authors note possible confounding with problem difficulty.
findings.measure: LO2 score and time on accurate hypothesis construction items

findings.finding_summary: A Wilcoxon signed-rank test showed a significant 15% increase in self-rated confidence in debugging after using HypoCompass (p = 0.007). Participants also rated the tool as significantly more engaging (6.0/7), fun (6.0/7), and less frustrating (2.5/7) than their conventional way of learning debugging and testing (p < 0.005 for each).
findings.measure: Self-rated debugging confidence and experience ratings (engaging, fun, frustrating)
findings.effect_size: 15% increase in confidence; engagement=6.0/7; fun=6.0/7; frustration=2.5/7

findings.finding_summary: In the LLM evaluation study, expert inspections across 6 practice problems and 145 buggy programs found that HypoCompass achieved a 90% success rate in generating and validating a complete set of materials. A complete set could be produced with only about 15 minutes of labeling and editing, and the LLM-assisted workflow was reported as 4.67 times less time-intensive than human TA generation.
findings.measure: Instructional material generation success rate and time/instructor overhead
findings.effect_size: 90% success rate; 4.67x less time than human TAs

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI GPT-family large language models used for text and code generation.
identified_tools.use_case: Used within HypoCompass's material-generation pipeline: gpt-3.5-turbo generated most materials and GPT-4 generated bug explanations/fix instructions; evaluated for quality and efficiency of producing hints, buggy code, explanations, and fixes.

findings.finding_summary: Using OpenAI models in the generation pipeline, the system produced high-quality materials with strong reported success rates: test case description hints 98.36% (61 outputs), test case category hints 94.44% (18 outputs), bug explanation and fix 91.72% (145 outputs), and bug fix 86.15% (195 outputs). The authors report that a complete set of practice materials could be generated with a 90% success rate and about 15 minutes of human labeling/editing.
findings.measure: Success rate of AI-generated instructional materials

findings.finding_summary: Compared with two experienced human CS TAs, the LLM-assisted workflow required substantially less time to produce one set of practice materials. Human TA generation took around 60 minutes plus 11 minutes evaluation, whereas the paper states LLM-based generation and editing required 4.67 times less time.
findings.measure: Time to generate one set of instructional materials

findings.finding_summary: Prompt engineering improved generation quality within the OpenAI-based pipeline. Reframing local bug fixing as a translation task reduced over-fixing errors by 70%, and hierarchical prompt disentanglement for bug explanation/fix instruction improved success rates by over 40%.
findings.measure: Generation error rate and prompt success rate
findings.effect_size: 70% reduction in over-fixing errors; over 40% improvement in success rates

quality_tier_rationale: The paper includes an empirical pre-post study with n=19 and a separate system-generation evaluation, but it lacks a randomized or controlled comparison condition for learning outcomes. Evidence is promising yet based on a small in-lab single-group design with some qualitative/self-report measures.
impact_tier_rationale: Reported learning gains are modest but statistically significant, including an 11.7% score improvement and 13.6% time reduction, plus a 15% confidence increase. However, standardized effect sizes are not reported, so impact is best classified as modest rather than clearly large.
